extracted.intended_audience: general readers, writers, and literature students interested in epistolary fiction
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and descriptive criteria for composing or analysing novels told through letters and other diegetic documents, including classical examples, devices, and modern permutations (emails, transcripts, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of letters and fictional documents as primary narrative form
rubrics_metrics.description: A novel written as a series of letters between fictional characters; the term often extends to novels that intersperse other kinds of fictional documents (diary entries, newspaper clippings, transcripts) with the letters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include any documents that can plausibly exist diegetically within the characters' lives; modern epistolaries may also include electronic documents (emails, blog posts, recordings). Examples: traditional letters (Clarissa), diary entries (Frankenstein), newspaper clippings and transcripts (Dracula, Illuminae).

rubrics_metrics.name: Diegetic realism (text exists within characters' lives)
rubrics_metrics.description: The epistolary form can add greater realism to a story because the text exists diegetically within the lives of the characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leverage the fact that documents are authored by characters to ground events concretely in the world of the story; preserve internal details and material aspects (handwriting, delivery) when appropriate to enhance authenticity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrating differing points of view without an omniscient narrator
rubrics_metrics.description: Epistolaries are particularly able to demonstrate differing points of view without recourse to an omniscient narrator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use multiple correspondents and their subjective letters to reveal contrasts in perception, knowledge, and motivation rather than summarising events from an outside voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fictional editor as authenticity device
rubrics_metrics.description: An important strategic device in the epistolary novel for creating the impression of authenticity is the fictional editor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame the collected documents with editorial notes, anthology framing, or comments that plausibly explain selection, ordering, or redaction to increase the reader's suspension of disbelief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Letters as central plot-construction mechanism
rubrics_metrics.description: Letters are central to plot construction across epistolary works; intercepts, misdeliveries, and copied messages catalyze reversals and reveal private motives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use material contingencies of letter-exchange (lost letters, misrouting, censorship) as plot devices to create misunderstandings, revelations, or reversals; e.g., intercepted or delayed letters that change characters' fortunes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Epistolary scaffolding as a narratological feature
rubrics_metrics.description: The epistolary scaffolding is systematic enough to be treated as a narratological feature of the genre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the form (sequence of documents, gaps, dates, voice shifts) as a structural element that shapes pacing, information flow, and temporal perspective rather than a mere gimmick.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of dramatic devices: forged, withheld, or misdelivered letters
rubrics_metrics.description: Common epistolary devices include letters that fall into the wrong hands, faked letters, or letters withheld by protagonists, which produce intrigue and plot complications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ forgeries, suppression, or misdelivery deliberately to generate tension or irony; be mindful that such devices can feel contrived if overused or insufficiently motivated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types by number of correspondents (monophonic, dialogic, polyphonic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Epistolary novels can be categorized based on the number of people whose letters are included: monophonic (one character), dialogic (two characters), polyphonic (three or more).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose the number of voices to suit narrative aims: monophonic for intimate interiority, dialogic for focused relationship dynamics, polyphonic for wider social panoramas and competing perspectives. Examples: monophonic—The Sorrows of Young Werther; dialogic—Letters of Fanni Butler; polyphonic—Dracula.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discrepant awareness in polyphonic epistolary novels
rubrics_metrics.description: A crucial element in polyphonic epistolary novels is 'discrepant awareness': simultaneous but separate correspondences create dramatic tension by giving characters different knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exploit mismatched knowledge across letters to create irony and suspense—what one character knows in a letter should contrast with what another reveals elsewhere to produce dramatic effects (used in Clarissa, Les Liaisons dangereuses).

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification by inclusion and type of non-letter documents
rubrics_metrics.description: Epistolary novels may be classified according to the type and quantity of use of non-letter documents (diaries, newspaper clippings, transcripts, telegrams, logs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mix document types to vary perspective and genre tone (e.g., newspaper clippings for public perspective, diaries for private reflection, transcripts for forensic or documentary feel). Consider plausibility of each document type within the story world.

rubrics_metrics.name: Framing devices and nested narratives
rubrics_metrics.description: Epistolary works frequently use framing devices—letters may form a frame story or contain nested narratives told through documents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use outer frames (a sea captain's log, an editor's preface) to contextualise inner accounts, mediate reliability, or provide temporal distance (e.g., Frankenstein's multiple framing letters). Be explicit about who collects or preserves documents to justify the compilation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Voice, addressivity, and first-person correspondence
rubrics_metrics.description: Epistolary fiction explores voice and addressivity through first-person correspondence, allowing intimate exploration of desire, subjectivity, and rhetorical address (as in Ovid's Heroides).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Craft distinct voices for letter-writers; attend to how each writer addresses recipients (tone, rhetorical strategies); use changes in voice to show character development or deteriorating mental states (e.g., Flowers for Algernon’s progress reports).

rubrics_metrics.name: Permutation into modern electronic and found-document modalities
rubrics_metrics.description: More recently, epistolaries may include electronic documents such as recordings and radio, blog posts, emails, PowerPoint presentations, and transcripts—extending the form beyond handwritten letters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adapt the epistolary logic to new media—consider differences in register, metadata (timestamps, headers), and modes of circulation (public posts vs private emails). Examples: emails and posts in Where'd You Go, Bernadette; transcripts and classified documents in Illuminae.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre flexibility and suitability for satire, romance, detective fiction, etc.
rubrics_metrics.description: The epistolary form has been used across genres—romance, satire, detective fiction, political satire—and can be adapted to varied narrative aims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match document types and voice to genre conventions (e.g., detective stories may favor multiple documents and reports; satire may use letter-collections to parody social mores). Historical examples: Lettres persanes (satire), The Moonstone (detective), Les Liaisons dangereuses (social/psychological drama).

rubrics_metrics.name: Susceptibility to parody and burlesque
rubrics_metrics.description: Starting in the 18th century the epistolary form attracted parody and burlesque (e.g., Fielding's Shamela) because melodramatic diary/letter entries can be lampooned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If aiming for sincerity, avoid overly contrived melodrama that courts parody; if aiming for satire, lean into epistolary tropes that invite parody (exaggerated emotion, implausible writing circumstances).
